newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to talk about economy and budget at G7 - MOF.
newsitem.headline: Japan to talk about economy and budget at G7 - MOF.

text.p: Finance Minister Wataru Kubo said on Friday that Japan would like to explain thoroughly that its economy is recovering but that it is facing tight finances to other Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations in Washington on Saturday.

"I am aware that countries such as the United States are requesting that Japan take economic stimulus steps. I would like to explain thoroughly about Japan's fiscal conditions and economic movements (at the G7 meeting)," Kubo told a regular news conference.
G7 finance ministers and central bank governors are due to meet in Washington on Saturday on the sidelines of the IMF/World Bank meeting.

"There is no change in our view that the Japanese economy is heading towards self-sustainable recovery based on private-sector demand, even though the pace of the recovery is gradual at the moment," he said.

At the same time, he said, Japan's government debt is remarkably large among those of the G7 nations, and if Tokyo adopts a large supplementary budget this year featuring public works spending to stimulate the economy, the debt would grow even larger.
In 1995/96, Japan formed a 14 trillion yen package of economic stimulus steps.
"Japan has two issues to resolve -- rebuilding state finances and ensuring economic recovery. It is not correct to think of achieving just one of those goals," he said.
However, Kubo added that this did not necessarily mean Japan was never going to form another stimulus package.
"We have to decide which option to take while keeping our eyes on the two goals," he said.
Kubo reiterated an earlier remark that the government would not back down on a plan to raisee the three-percent consumption tax to five percent in April 1997.

"Concerning pensioners and those with low income, we have to consider them from the viewpoint of interest rates as well. We must tackle the issue of what social measures for them would be possible. We have not forgotten them," he said.
